Language is how one mind gets a piece of what is inside it across to another. A shared word is really a shared chunk of mental map: when two people are trained to the same word, they load roughly the same patch of 'how things are and could be.' Understanding does not require that your version be identical to mine, only close enough that we can coordinate, predict, and go on together. This is why teaching, writing, and specialist jargon all work: each installs a region of one person's map in another. And the gap between separate minds is not a flaw language has to defeat; it is the very thing language exists to cross: there has to be a gap for anything to be said across it.

::: {.identification}
**Language** · *Identification*

Language is the technology of shared interiority: the structured practice by which one mind externalizes a region of its modal field (§8.3) (a model, a claim, a refusal, a promise) into another mind's, across the interval that separates self-modeling minds. A shared word is a shared region of map; understanding is the sufficient reproduction of one field's structure in another, never identical, but enough to coordinate. The interval is not a barrier to that transfer but its condition: there must be a gap for a claim to cross.
*Status: an identity claim on the §7.8 self-modeling structure (Principle 5), defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

A will acting through its modal field (§8.9) eventually has to make the field legible to other actors. Language is the first technology of that making. The central question is not how sound, gesture, posture, or marks become meaningful, but how the structural content of one mind's model can be reliably transferred (imperfectly but systematically) into another's.

Language carries the claim while art (§8.13) carries the feel. Each depends on T, S, and Φ, requires self-modeling at both ends, and crosses the same interval under the same conditions. What distinguishes them is the content each is structured to carry, and the fact that each can carry what the other cannot. Language reaches as far as propositions reach. Beyond that boundary, the work belongs to art.

What language transfers, mechanically, is regions of the speaker's modal field (§8.3) into the hearer's. A shared vocabulary is a shared region of map: every speaker trained to a word has the same chunk of possibility space loaded under the same label. Jargon is what compressed labels look like for densely-mapped specialist regions: a single technical term invokes a region of modal field that took a discipline decades to lay down, available now in one syllable for anyone who has been trained into the region. This is why teaching is modal-representation installation, why documentation freezes a region for asynchronous transfer, and why a discipline's evolution toward shared vocabulary is, structurally, the formation of a consensus map across the bodies who practice it. The interval language crosses is the interval between maps; the fact that the same words can install nearly the same regions across millions of bodies is what makes coordinated knowledge possible at all.

*Communication's expressive and referential functions.* Communication runs on a continuum from pure expressive function (direct externalization of the sender's drive-state) to referential function: externalization of modeled objects in the sender's modal field, displaced from the immediate context. A cat backed into a corner rearing itself, a dog snarling, a bird's alarm call, a baby's cry, a wince at unexpected news: these are expressive; they make the sender's drive-state public so other beings can register and respond. Symbolic language carries the expressive function all the way up; "stop that" is functionally a snarl with words, "I love you" is functionally a purr with grammar, and a great deal of everyday speech is more articulated drive-state externalization than referential transmission. What symbolic language adds at sufficient depth is referential function: the capacity to externalize content that *is not* the sender's current drive-state, referents displaced from the here-and-now, other times, other places, hypothetical states, abstract types, counterfactual branches, the absent friend, last week's meeting, next year's plan, the square root of two. A cat cannot rear at the threat that was here yesterday or at the threat its modal field is projecting forward; the cat's body has no apparatus for that displacement. The recursion that performs displacement is the same modal-field machinery §8.4 named in its account of reasoning, applied here to externalize modal-field content rather than to operate on it internally. Referential function does not replace expressive function (almost all human utterance carries both), but it is the structural addition that emerges as the depth gradient deepens, gradually rather than at a sharp break. Vervet predator-calls have a thin form of reference (type-of-predator, not just here's-something-bad). Bee waggle dances have thin displacement (food at a location not currently visible). Toddler pointing at an absent ball is fuller displacement. Adult abstract reference is the upper end. The §8.10 section's specific work is on the deep-form referential capacity; its expressive function remains continuous with the signaling that runs all the way down the depth gradient.

Two self-modeling configurations persist, occupy genuinely different positions, and remain in causal exchange across the interval between them. Distinction, persistence, succession (Spatiality, Physicality, Temporality) are not features the linguistic situation happens to require. They are what propositional transmission consists in. Without distinct positions, there is no separation for a claim to cross. Without persistence, there is no speaker whose claim remains the same claim a hearer can take up. Without succession, there is no before-and-after to the act of saying or the act of being understood. A proposition is a structure that can survive the journey between minds because the journey passes through the same three conditions every other concrete transition passes through. The exchange can hold content mutually across the interval: each speaker contributes to what the other can take up, rather than merely passing an asymmetric signal. Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, §8.3) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of collectively held knowledge; language is one means by which such knowledge can be formed and transmitted, not an automatic application of the theorem.

This relocates the standing positions in philosophy of language. Saussure's conventional signs, Chomsky's generative competence, Wittgenstein's meaning as use, Frege's sense and reference, Kripke's rigid designation, and Davidson's truth-conditional semantics were each tracking real features of how minds reach each other through propositional form. What the structural account corrects is the assumption common to all of them: that language is a system separable from the structure it describes, a layer of signs or rules or uses that coordinates with reality through some external relation. Language is not separable. Its structure is the structure it carries because there is no other structure for it to carry, and what each tradition was tracking is what propositional transmission looks like from the angle that tradition approached. That there is a mind-independent structure for language to carry, rather than a scheme the mind lays over a formless content, is the realism defended once at §8.4.

The charitable readings sharpen the point. Wittgenstein (1953) is right that meaning is bound to use: a proposition that does not function in the practice of any community of speakers does not transmit, because there are no shared procedures by which a hearer can recover its content. Kripke (1980) is right that names refer through causal-historical chains rather than through descriptions speakers can articulate, because reference must survive disagreement and error about what is being referred to. Davidson (1967, 1973) is right that the systematic compositionality of truth-conditions is what makes infinite production from finite resources possible: recursive grammar is the structural feature that lets propositions of arbitrary complexity transmit without each one requiring a new convention. Quine (1960) is right that translation underdetermines: no observable behavior fully fixes the model in another speaker's mind; the gap between minds is real, and what closes it sufficiently is alignment under shared conditions rather than identity of internal representation. Chomsky (1965, 1986) is right that linguistic competence requires the recursive structure linguistics describes, because that recursion is what allows propositions to embed propositions: the structural condition for any speaker to articulate a thought *about* what another speaker has said. Each position locates one face of the same structural fact: a configuration capable of modeling itself, modeling another, and modeling what passes between them must coordinate across distinct positions, across time, and across whatever sustains the exchange. Where the literature has competed over which face is fundamental, the structural account reads them as views of one transmission from different angles.

*The private-language pressure.* One charitable credit is not yet an answer to Wittgenstein's private-language challenge, and the section's own vocabulary is what stands exposed to it. If "shared interiority" named a private inner sample each speaker checks a word against, the private-language argument (Wittgenstein 1953, §§243–315) would apply in full: nothing could count as using the label correctly, and "the same chunk of possibility space under the same label" would carry exactly the confusion the argument diagnoses. The concession is total: there is no private sample. The interior §7.8 derives is not an object held up against a word but a self-modeling process whose contents are individuated by what they let a configuration do: coordinate, correct, predict, and go on. So the criteria for two speakers having loaded the same region are public, where Wittgenstein placed them: convergence under shared conditions and continued success in use, not an inward comparison no one could check. Rule-following and forms of life are then not pressures the account must absorb from outside; they name the same fact from the side of practice: a region of modal field counts as shared when, and only when, the practice of using it holds up across the interval. Family resemblance operates by the same standard: concept boundaries are fixed by overlapping use rather than shared essence, so whether a modal-map region coheres is judged by whether use holds together, not by whether a common property subtends it. The structural account does not posit an inside the criteria fail to reach. It locates the inside as the publicly-criterioned thing Wittgenstein's own argument requires.

*A test case: acquaintance without articulation.* Consider a child raised in total isolation from language, encountering water directly, with no interlocutor and no word ever offered. Such a child registers the wet/dry distinction: the same thermal-and-mechanical inference apparatus that produces the sensation in any human body runs whether or not a word exists for its output, and a dog or a fish, with no language at all, plainly responds differently to being wet and being dry. What the isolated child lacks is not the sensation but the shared criterion: a public practice of using a label reliably enough that another speaker could correct a misuse. This is a thin registration, in the depth-gradient sense running through this chapter: a real discrimination, held by the system, that has not yet been articulated, named, or folded into a practice checkable by anyone else. The private-language argument's target was never the existence of that thin registration; it was the idea of a private sample a word could be privately checked against. The isolated child has the registration and no word; what would be incoherent is a claim to have privately named it in a sense no one, including a later-taught version of the same child, could ever get right or wrong. Helen Keller's own account of the moment at the water pump makes the transition vivid: the sensation of water over her hand was already fully present long before language, and what broke open at the pump was not a new feeling but the discovery that the finger-spelled pattern named the thing she had been feeling all along — the folding of a thin registration into the public, checkable practice a word requires.

Language has structure because that is what language describes. The claim is about the deep conditions of propositional transmission (reference, predication, recursion across an interval), not about surface grammars, lexicons, idioms, or inflectional systems, which are shaped by historical contingencies the structural account does not track. The conditions any language must meet to carry propositions across the interval between speakers are the same conditions a self-modeling being must meet to register anything at all. If consciousness is a self-modeling process registering itself from inside, and language is the practice by which that self-registration is articulated and shared, then the structure of language is the process's own logical form, made communicable. The proof required all three roles to state itself; language requires the same three to carry any statement at all. The derivation and linguistic practice arrived at the same grammar. Every sentence that successfully says anything (in any language, by any species capable of uttering one) runs on the same structural conditions the argument has named, from whatever position within them the speaker happens to occupy.

The depth-gradient framing applies to language as it does to other registers. Many species transmit information via signals: pheromone trails (ants), referential alarm calls (vervets; Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980), waggle dances (bees), individual signature whistles (dolphins), prairie-dog calls apparently encoding predator type, size, and color (Slobodchikoff 2002). These are shallow forms of language: signaling without recursive grammar, displacement, or full theory-of-mind dependence. Full propositional language with recursive embedding emerges most fully in humans, who have the recursive depth required to model others as modelers and the symbolic capacity to externalize that modeling. The shallow forms exist below the self-aware threshold the chapter's opening names; the deep form requires it.

*Gossip as a primary social use of language.* Among the deep-form referential uses of language, gossip (talking-about-other-people, especially people in proximity, especially regarding their conduct) has structural prominence. Dunbar's *Grooming, Gossip, and the Evolution of Language* (1996) argued that the small-group social-information-sharing function predates and underwrites the more abstract referential uses humans developed; the 150-person Dunbar number is the social-information-management scale where gossip operates natively. Read in the modal-field vocabulary, gossip is *distributed modal-field maintenance* for a social network. It delivers actualities about specific people in the listener's proximity (what they did, how they responded, what they value) at higher proximity-weighting than distant or fictional cases, because the modal apparatus treats nearby actualities as more applicable to the body's own field than far ones. It maps consequences as well as actualities: shame, ostracism, reputational damage, social cost (the visible consequences of conduct gossip names) are what make gossip an effective norm-enforcement mechanism. It is also a distributed predator-detection system: a body that has heard the right gossip can recognize an exploitative neighbor, a manipulator, or an untrustworthy partner without being burned individually. Reputation, the structure gossip lays down, is itself a feature of the social modal field (everyone's prediction of how a given person is likely to behave), and gossip is the substrate by which that structure is built and updated. This is one of the reasons gossip is reflexively pleasurable across cultures: the modal apparatus is being fed exactly what it is hungry for, in a domain it cares about deeply (immediate social possibility), at evidential weight high enough to be useful. Reality TV, true crime, celebrity coverage, and social-media commentary are extensions of the same operation at scale, mediated by technologies that broaden the proximity-circle the apparatus treats as relevant; the underlying drive is the modal-field-expansion drive §8.1 names, here flowing through the referential function of language at the social register where Dunbar located its evolutionary purpose. Beyond the evolutionary register Dunbar names, gossip is also where social categories are constituted and enforced: reputations, roles, and standings are the ameliorative kinds of §8.10.1 maintained in distributed talk, and to gossip about how someone occupied a role is to keep updating the social modal field that says what the role demands.

*Pronouns and the register collision.* A pronoun is the most compressed referential device a language has for a person: in a single syllable it installs, in the hearer's modal field, a minimal re-identifiable position for the referent — a shared region of map at its smallest. In gendered languages that installation bundles a social-category assignment into the act of referring, which is why the pronoun becomes a site of dispute out of all proportion to its size: three registers meet in one word. Using a pronoun is a referential-and-social-category act (§8.10.1); the identity it points at is a self-model position (§8.5); the body it may or may not track is the substrate (§8.6). Much of the contemporary argument is a register collision — parties who take the pronoun to report a substrate fact, parties who take it to register a self-model position, and parties who take it to maintain an ameliorative social kind are not contradicting one another about a single thing but speaking across three. What the structural account settles is narrow and firm: whom the pronoun refers to is a subject whose standing is fixed at §8.12 by the capacity for experience, not by category-membership, so the referring-verdict — that there is a someone here, owed what any subject is owed — is invariant across the readings. What it does not settle is the contested etiquette and policy specifics of who is owed which term under which conditions; that adjudication is not the structural account's to make. The deeper point answers the natural puzzle of why anything has a pronoun at all: reference across the interval requires re-identifiable positions, since distinction, persistence, and succession are what let a claim about a someone survive the trip between minds, and a pronoun is the minimal such re-identifier. In that sense a pronoun is structural. Its gender-marking is not — gendered pronouns are surface grammar, among the historical contingencies this section has already set aside as untracked by the structural claim — but contingent at the grammatical layer is not trivial at the personal layer: the self-model position a pronoun references (§8.5) is real and consequential even where the grammatical gender-slot that carries it is arbitrary. The deep fact, that reference needs a re-identifiable position, is invariant; the gendered packaging of that position is contingent. Much of the heat around pronouns, like the older habit of assigning the ungendered a default gendered term, is a contingent grammatical slot being mistaken for a substrate verdict.

*In-group vocabulary and modal-field narrowing.* Not every installation a shared vocabulary performs is expansive. A term can install a region of social possibility by closing a hearer's field rather than opening it: labeling one's own group *the elect*, *the remnant*, or *the light of the world* installs a favorable self-location that need not be argued for each time it is invoked, and labeling disagreement *worldliness*, *hardness of heart*, or *suppression of the truth* installs an unfavorable location for the response before its content is examined. Maxims that foreclose a line of inference before it opens — *God works in mysterious ways*, *who are we to question*, *just have faith* — do compressed referential work the way a pronoun does at smaller scale, loaded once and then spent without argument on every later occasion. What is distinctive about this class is the direction of the installation: most vocabulary opens a region of the hearer's field for use, the way jargon makes a decade of a discipline's mapping available in one syllable; this class installs a boundary against further mapping, marking a region closed rather than making one available. The pattern is not specific to any one tradition or doctrine. Structurally identical devices recur across independent religious and political traditions wherever a group's boundary needs maintaining at lower cost than argument supplies, which is what makes the convergence a corroboration rather than an argument in its own right: it is what this section's account of language predicts language will be recruited to do wherever groups form and hold boundaries, not a separate case against whichever group happens to be doing it.

Successful communication is not merely the transfer of information; it is the convergence of two minds' models on a shared claim about Nature they both inhabit. The interval between speakers is not a barrier to that convergence but its condition: there must be a gap for a claim to cross. Understanding is the confirmation that the structural content of one model has been reproduced in another, not identically, but sufficiently for coordination. That reproducibility is what the structural account of language predicts and what the experience of being understood reports.

*A note on scope.* This identification (language as the structured practice by which propositional content crosses the interval between self-modeling persons) is offered as a structural account of what language is, not as a strict derivation from the proof of Chapters 1–2. The proof establishes the necessary structural conditions T, S, and Φ; the claim that those conditions are what propositional transmission consists in at the depth a self-modeling configuration reaches is an identification claim, in the sense flagged at the head of Chapter 8. That a reader might accept the proof while reading the linguistic case differently (assigning more weight to convention, to use, to neural architecture, or to social practice) leaves nothing earlier disturbed; the identification carries weight just to the degree it fits the phenomenon.
